verdicts.summary: Lean has an equivalent formula. The Lean states the resolved recursion, not the increment. It takes one degree m for every input jet of order ≤ N (‖D^J A‖ ≤ K·S^m, i.e. c_J = m, and ‖D^I g‖ ≤ w·K·S^m·P, i.e. b_I = m), and concludes with the slot exponent (m+1)(n+1) at order n. That is exactly the solution of the paper's recursion in that case: the zeroth bound carries S^{m+1} (amplitude_le_polynomial at n = 0, the extra power being the slot length L_s ≤ K·S), and 1 + max{m, max_{0<J≤I}(m + b'_{I−J})} = 1 + m + b'_{I−1}, so b'_I = (m+1)(I+1). When the paper's degrees genuinely vary with the order, the Lean hypothesis is met by taking m to be the maximum of the finitely many input degrees b_I and c_J for orders ≤ N. That is harmless because (7.14)-(7.15) assert only that some finite degrees work ('Constants and degrees may depend on M, I, and the prescribed source bounds', p. 78), so a coarser common degree still yields a conclusion of the same form, with exponent at least the paper's finer b'_I. (The paper's sentence after this display, 'The inverse-distance exponent can be enlarged to the maximum of the source and lower-order exponents', concerns the δ^{-a'_I} exponent of (7.14)/(7.15), not this S_*-degree, so it is not what licenses the uniform K·S^m hypothesis.) Nothing downstream needs more than a finite degree. norm_jet_solution_le keeps the increment in unresolved product form: one factor Q = 1 + C·L·2^N·M per derivative, where 2^N·M is the coefficient-jet bound, which is the paper's per-step increase before the degrees are counted.
